newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Poll shows Romania's Iliescu in election trouble.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows Romania's Iliescu in election trouble.

text.p: A new opinion survey by Romania's most respected polling institute published on Tuesday showed President Ion Iliescu losing ground in the final stages of the campaign for Sunday's election.

Iliescu was campaigning in Brasov, north of the capital, where he ran into fresh protests against the plunge in living standards during his seven years of power since the execution of Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

The survey published in three newspapers gave Iliescu 29 percent of the vote - three points more than academic Emil Constantinescu and well short of the 50 percent needed for victory without a run-off. Former Prime Minister Petre Roman was third in the field of 16 with 20 percent.

The margin was the smallest in Iliescu's favour since the beginning of a bruising campaign marked by personal attacks and accusations that Iliescu and his ruling Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) were plotting mass fraud.
In parliamentary elections also to be held on Sunday, the poll detected little change, with the PDSR running second, six points behind Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR).

The survey was conducted by the IRSOP institute, which better reflects rural areas and has proved the most accurate of Romania's erratic opinion polls in the past. The newspapers said it was originally intended for internal use and IRSOP officials confirmed the figures were theirs.

Since the end of Communism, Romania's living standards and industrial indicators have lagged far behind its neighbours. Average monthly wages stand at the equivalent of less than $100, one-third of those in Poland.
Rivals say Iliescu is a leftover from a Communist system which has yet to be revamped and accuse him inflicting widespread poverty on the country of 23 million.
Romanian radio said Iliescu was confronted briefly at a Brasov tractor plant by about 50 protesters brandishing placards that read: "Enough of your Humbug!"
Iliescu has expressed confidence that he will be re-elected to a new four-year term. But news reports last week also said he had been jeered at other public meetings.

All 16 candidates, including a faith healer, the leaders of the Car Drivers' Party and Pensioners' Party and two rival Socialists, are to crowd into a television studio on Thursday for a 3-1/2 hour debate.
Romania's exiled King Michael, barred from entering the country since 1992, urged Romanians in an open letter to vote to maintain the rights won when communism collapsed.

"Seven years ago at the price of spilled blood you won the right to a free vote..." the King wrote from his headquarters in Switzerland. "The economic, social and cultural future depends on each one of you voting."
The king, who drew big crowds in 1992, is generally agreed to have little influence on the poll. But Iliescu's campaign spots suggest Constantinescu would back his return to power.
